common_name: Shimonita Negi Bunching Onion (Japanese Thick-Stemmed Grilling Onion)

planting.note: Sow in a nursery bed in spring, then transplant seedlings into a trench in early-to-mid summer, gradually backfilling and hilling soil around the stems through fall to blanch the thick white shank; a long cold period after the first hard frosts concentrates the sugars that make this variety famous.

directions: Shimonita Negi comes from Shimonita Town in Japan's Gunma Prefecture and, unlike most bunching onions, grows as a single thick, unbranched stalk rather than dividing into a clump of thin shoots. Transplant seedlings into a trench and progressively mound soil up the stem over the growing season, a technique called hilling that blanches the shank to a diameter rivaling a small leek. It needs a long season, typically six to twelve months from sowing, and is traditionally harvested in late fall or early winter after frost has sweetened the stalk and softened its raw pungency into a mellow, umami-rich flavor. Use the thick blanched shanks whole in sukiyaki, nabe hot pots, and grilling, where the interior turns tender and almost custardy when cooked.

common_name: Red Welsh Onion (Red-Based Perennial Bunching Onion)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring once soil is workable, or in late summer for an overwintered clump; despite the name this is an Asian-origin perennial scallion, not a true Welsh native, and it is happy in cool weather at either end of the season.

directions: Red Welsh Onion produces hollow, grey-green to blue-green stalks rising from a red-skinned, white-centered base, with the color deepening toward the root end rather than covering the whole plant. Harvest outer stalks continuously like scallions while leaving the center of each clump to keep growing, and expect the clump to widen to about a foot across in a single good season. Left unharvested into its second year, it sends up tall flowering stems topped with off-white globe-shaped flower heads that are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators, after which the clump can be divided to renew vigor and start new plantings. It tolerates a wide range of garden soils and, once established, can often be harvested in some form in every season of the year.

planting.note: Sow true seed indoors in trays or modules 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping soil around 60F for best germination, then transplant hardened-off seedlings out once hard frosts have passed.

directions: Matador is a Dutch-bred F1 hybrid shallot grown from true seed rather than planted as clonal sets, a modern approach that avoids the virus buildup that can weaken old set-propagated shallot lines. Each seed-grown plant typically produces a broad, obovate pair of bulbs rather than the large multi-bulb cluster typical of open-pollinated shallots, with thick reddish-brown papery skin protecting crisp, richly flavored white flesh. Keep the bed evenly moist through spring growth and reduce watering as the foliage yellows and topples over in midsummer, then lift and cure the bulbs in a warm, airy spot for storage. Matador is widely offered by seed companies on both sides of the Atlantic and is valued for consistently heavy, uniform yields.

planting.note: Start true seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out as soon as the ground can be worked; Conservor is bred by Bejo Seeds and is sold as seed rather than sets through most seed catalogs.

directions: Conservor is a French-type F1 hybrid shallot with an elongated, slightly teardrop shape, papery reddish-copper skin, and deep pink-tinged flesh. Unlike many shallots it tends to stay as a single large bulb or split into just two rather than dividing into a big cluster, and the skin peels away cleanly in one motion without papery material trapped between doubled bulbs. It has a fine texture and a delicate flavor between onion and garlic, and it is prized above all for exceptional storage life, commonly keeping for many months longer than standard shallots when properly cured. Reduce watering once the tops yellow and fall over, then cure in a warm, airy spot before storing.

planting.note: Plant sets about an inch deep and four to six inches apart as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Pikant is among the fastest-maturing shallot sets commonly grown.

directions: Pikant is a widely grown European set-shallot producing clusters of medium-sized, slightly elongated bulbs wrapped in rich copper-red to mahogany papery skin over red-tinged flesh. Its flavor is noticeably more pungent and assertive than the milder Dutch Yellow types, as its name suggests, which makes it a favorite where a stronger shallot bite is wanted in cooking. Plant sets shallowly in loose, well-drained soil and keep the row weed-free while bulbs size up through late spring and early summer. Pikant matures quickly for a shallot and, once cured, keeps for an unusually long stretch in cool, dry storage.
sources: Crate and Basket shallot variety guide

planting.note: Start true seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off; unlike most shallot varieties Ed's Red is open-pollinated and bulks up to full size from seed in a single season rather than from replanted clonal sets.

directions: Ed's Red is an open-pollinated, true-seed shallot improved by farmer-breeder Beth Rasgorshek of Nampa, Idaho, grown fresh from seed each year rather than propagated as replanted clonal sets. It produces larger-than-typical, dark crimson-skinned bulbs with mild, pink-ringed flesh, and is notably productive for a seed-grown shallot. Reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over, then lift, cure in a warm airy spot, and store; Ed's Red is prized for exceptionally long keeping, often reported to hold firm for the better part of a year. Because it is grown fresh from seed each season, it sidesteps much of the virus buildup that can shorten the vigor of old clonally propagated shallot strains.

planting.note: Start true seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off, the same way as other seed-grown F1 shallots.

directions: Innovator is a Conservor-type F1 hybrid true-seed shallot producing elongated, mostly single bulbs with reddish-bronze papery skin, bred with improved field tolerance to downy mildew compared with older shallot lines. Start it indoors and transplant like other seed-grown shallots rather than planting it from sets, keeping the bed evenly moist during establishment and tapering off water as the tops begin to yellow and fall. It is suited to both fresh-market use and long-term storage, and its disease tolerance makes it a reliable choice in regions where downy mildew pressure on alliums runs high.

planting.note: Start true seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once hardened off; seed-grown Creation bulbs typically reach harvest a week or two later than set-grown French-Italian type shallots.

directions: Creation is a European F1 hybrid true-seed shallot of the French-Italian type, producing relatively small, soft-tasting bulbs roughly an inch to an inch and three-quarters across that are easy to peel and quick to store. Being seed-propagated rather than grown from sets, it avoids much of the virus carryover that can affect older clonal shallot stock, though the bulbs mature slightly later than set-grown shallots of similar type. Reduce watering as foliage yellows and falls over, then cure the harvest in a warm, airy location before storing in a cool, dry place.

common_name: Roderique Shallot (French Banana-Type Louisiana Creole Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in mild-winter regions for a late-spring harvest, as is traditional in south Louisiana, or in very early spring where winters are severe.

directions: Roderique is a French banana-type shallot that French settlers brought to south Louisiana in the 1700s, where it became a Creole kitchen-garden staple still grown from saved bulb divisions rather than seed. Its tall, narrow, uniformly copper-skinned bulbs are white-fleshed and quick to peel with a single slice up the side, and each planted bulb is a highly productive multiplier, typically dividing into six to twelve new shallots in a season. Reduce watering once the foliage yellows and falls over, then lift, cure in a warm airy spot, and store; properly cured bulbs keep for nine to twelve months, among the longest storage life of any shallot type. Save a portion of the best bulbs each year to replant and keep the heirloom line going.

common_name: Green Mountain Multiplier Onion (Large-Bulbed Potato Onion)

planting.note: Plant small saved bulbs in fall for the largest harvest the following summer in mild-winter regions, or in very early spring as soon as soil is workable where winters are severe.

directions: Green Mountain Multiplier is a modern potato-onion selection developed around the year 2000 by Utah onion breeder Kelly Winterton from a chance flowering and seedling generation of the heirloom Yellow Potato Onion. It was selected and named for producing notably larger bulbs than most multiplier onions, approaching the size of a regular storage onion while keeping the multiplying, cluster-forming habit that defines potato onions. Set small bulbs about two inches deep with the tip near the soil surface; each one divides underground into a cluster of new bulbs by midsummer. Harvest once the tops die back, saving the largest bulbs to replant for next year's crop; true seed is also increasingly offered by specialty growers for gardeners who want to breed their own strains or refresh stock without carrying over soil-borne disease.

common_name: Moritz Walking Onion (Large-Topset Tree Onion Strain)

planting.note: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; spring planting also works but fall planting produces a larger clump sooner.

directions: Moritz is a heirloom strain of Egyptian walking onion distinguished by unusually large topset bulbils with a deeper red-purple blush than the common strain, and by occasionally producing a secondary whorl of bulbils partway up the flowering stalk in addition to the main cluster at the tip. Otherwise it is grown exactly like other walking onions: plant the topset bulbils an inch or two deep in fall, harvest green tops continuously through the season like scallions, and dig the small underground bulbs once the foliage begins to die back. As the topset clusters grow heavy, the stalk bends over and the bulbils root where they touch soil, letting the clump slowly migrate and expand the planting without any replanting needed. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep the strain vigorous and true to type.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom onion archive

common_name: Heritage White Walking Onion (Heritage Sweet Topsetting Onion)

planting.note: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; bulbils of this strain mature and ship later in the fall than many other walking onion strains.

directions: Heritage White is a pigment-free strain of Egyptian walking onion whose topset bulbils stay ivory-white to pale green with no red or purple blush anywhere on the plant, unlike most walking onion strains, which show at least some color. Growers favor it for a notably milder, sweeter flavor than the common strain, both in the underground bulbs and the aerial topsets. It is planted and managed the same way as other walking onions: set the topset bulbils an inch or two deep in fall, harvest hollow green tops through the season like scallions, and dig the small underground bulbs once the foliage dies back. Left undisturbed, the heavy topset clusters bend the flowering stalk to the ground and root themselves, letting the clump expand on its own year after year.
